C001.name: Differential programming
C001.definition: Differential programming is a programming paradigm where parts of the program are parameterized. This allows gradient-based optimization to tune those parameters to optimize the program or find a local optimum.

C002.name: Pointwise non-linearity
C002.definition: Pointwise non-linearity is a type of non-linearity where the function is applied to each component of the output vector individually. These non-linearities are usually applied element-wise.

C003.name: Generative model
C003.definition: Generative model is a type of model used to create new content, such as text or images, based on learned patterns. These models can be text-based or image-based.

C004.name: Transfer learning
C004.definition: Transfer learning is the technique of reusing components from a previously trained model. This allows knowledge learned for one task, such as categorizing animals, to be applied to a different task, like satellite imagery.

C005.name: Deep learning
C005.definition: Deep learning is a field of study interested in modeling complex phenomena in the real world. It is presented as a possible solution for tackling the difficulty of modeling these complex systems.

C006.name: Complex phenomena
C006.definition: Complex phenomena are real-world subjects that students interact with daily, such as natural language, images, videos, DNA, ecosystems, and climate change. These phenomena are difficult to model using traditional methods.

C007.name: Artificial Intelligence
C007.definition: AI is a field of study whose history the instructor will briefly go over. It is the broader domain within which deep learning operates.

C008.name: Perceptron
C008.definition: Perceptron is the first neural network, which was designed to recognize or categorize images. This basic unit forms the building block for most of the deep learning used today.

C009.name: Backpropagation
C009.definition: Backpropagation is a fundamental concept that enables multilayer perceptrons to be reasonably trained. This concept allows a gradient to be propagated through multiple layers of perceptrons.

C010.name: Multilayer perceptron
C010.definition: Multilayer perceptron is a structure consisting of multiple perceptrons stacked on top of each other. This structure allows the network to solve categorization problems that are not separable from a linear classifier.

C011.name: Convolutional neural network
C011.definition: Convolutional neural network (CNN) is a network architecture where earlier layers produce low-level representations, while later layers combine these into more complex representations.

C012.name: ImageNet
C012.definition: ImageNet is a very large-scale dataset of its kind. This dataset was a vital component that allowed machine learning to begin working effectively.

C013.name: Non-linearity
C013.definition: Non-linearity is the function applied between layers that allows a network to model complex, non-straight relationships. Without this non-linearity, stacking multiple linear layers simply results in a single linear combination.

C014.name: Modular reuse
C014.definition: Modular reuse is the concept within an open source community where trained weights from one architecture can be taken and used as a module within a larger system. This larger system may incorporate many different components pulled from various sources.

C015.name: Gradient descent
C015.definition: Gradient descent is the idea of optimizing a cost function by finding a minimum over the training data. This minimum is a set of parameters where the loss is minimized for all data points, aiming to find the optimal set of model parameters.

C016.name: Parameter
C016.definition: Parameters of a model are all the different layers of weights and biases that the model uses. These parameters are the values that the model adjusts during the learning process.

C017.name: Linear layer
C017.definition: Linear layer is a building block in neural networks where a component of the output representation is calculated as a sum over inputs multiplied by corresponding weights. This calculation can also incorporate a bias term.

C018.name: Bias term
C018.definition: Bias term is a component added to the calculation that does not take in any of the input components. It serves as a constant offset in the linear combination.

C019.name: Rectified linear unit
C019.definition: Rectified linear unit (ReLU) is a pointwise non-linearity defined as the maximum of zero and the input value $z$. This function is super efficient to implement and is widely used in current models.

C020.name: Representational power
C020.definition: Representational power is the theoretical ability of a model to map and represent complex functions. With two or more layers and non-linearity, a deep network can theoretically represent any function.

C021.name: Capacity
C021.definition: Capacity refers to the amount of complexity or number of dimensions a model can handle. Given sufficient capacity, a model can theoretically approximate any function.

C022.name: Deep network
C022.definition: Deep network is a type of neural network that represents data in a more compact way, allowing it to encode knowledge efficiently. This representation is considered an improvement over previous methods like lookup tables.

C023.name: Shallow network
C023.definition: Shallow network is a network structure that, if not sufficiently wide, may only be able to efficiently compute simple tasks, such as finding edges. In contrast, a deep network can efficiently compute much harder tasks.

C024.name: Overparameterized
C024.definition: Overparameterized describes a new paradigm in deep learning, replacing the classical concepts of underfitting and overfitting. This term refers to models that possess a very large number of parameters.

C025.name: Generalize
C025.definition: Generalize is the ability of a model to learn rules that apply broadly, rather than merely memorizing the training data. This allows the model to perform well on data that it has not seen before.

C026.name: Overfitting
C026.definition: Overfitting is the phenomenon where a model learns patterns from the training data so perfectly that it generalizes poorly to new, unseen data. This occurs when the model is too complex, resulting in a 'spiky' or 'peaky' function that fits the training points exactly.

C027.name: Cross-entropy loss
C027.definition: Cross-entropy loss is a function used to measure the distance between the distribution the model predicts and the actual distribution of the input. It forces the network to maximize the probability of the training data, thereby ensuring the output is a reasonable probability model of the object.

C028.name: One hot encoding
C028.definition: One hot encoding is a vector representation used for the ground truth label, where every element is zero except for the correct class, which is marked with a one.

C029.name: Tensor
C029.definition: A tensor is a multi-dimensional matrix that serves as the mathematical representation of the input data and the layers within the model. Essentially, everything in the deep learning model is represented as a tensor.

C030.name: Representation learning
C030.definition: Representation learning is the process of structuring data so that the network can learn concepts. This learning is studied through methods such as reconstruction and similarity.

C031.name: Neural network
C031.definition: Neural network is a structure consisting of a chain of different blocks or layers. Each of these layers has associated parameters that are used during the training process.

C032.name: Loss
C032.definition: Loss is a function used at the end of the network to calculate the cost. This cost is then used when thinking about the learning process.

C033.name: Optimal set of theta
C033.definition: Optimal set of theta is the specific set of parameters that minimizes the loss function. This minimization must occur across all of the available data set.

C034.name: Cost function
C034.definition: Cost function is a measure that quantifies the total loss across all data points in the training data set, which gradient descent seeks to minimize.

C035.name: Gradient
C035.definition: Gradient is a mathematical measure that indicates the direction of maximal change for a parameter set, which is used in optimization algorithms.

C036.name: Learning rate (eta)
C036.definition: Learning rate (eta) is a defined value that determines how far the parameters will step in the direction of the gradient during each iteration.

C037.name: Loss landscape
C037.definition: Loss landscape is the surface that represents the cost function, and it is where the optimization process begins and moves to find a minimum.

C038.name: Global minimum
C038.definition: Global minimum is the single lowest point in the entire loss landscape, representing the optimal solution that minimizes the loss function across all possible parameter settings.

C039.name: Stochastic gradient descent
C039.definition: Stochastic gradient descent is an optimization method that approximates the total gradient by calculating it over a small subset of the data. This approach is used because calculating the gradient over the entire dataset is often computationally intractable.

C040.name: Batch
C040.definition: A batch is a subset of the data that is used to compute the gradient at any given point during the training process. The size of the batch determines how many examples are used before the parameters are updated.

C041.name: Overall loss function
C041.definition: The overall loss function is the total measure of error that the model attempts to minimize. This function is typically calculated as a sum of the individual losses across every single example in the training data.

C042.name: Implicit regularizer
C042.definition: An implicit regularizer is a property of stochastic gradient descent where the inherent noise in the gradient calculation helps stabilize the training process. This noise can assist the model in finding a better solution.

C043.name: Local minima
C043.definition: Local minima is a point in the loss landscape where the function value is lower than all surrounding points, but this point is not necessarily the lowest possible point overall.

C044.name: Momentum
C044.definition: Momentum is a technique in gradient descent that biases gradient steps to continue in the direction of previous updates. This gives the optimization process momentum based on its past direction of movement.

C045.name: Hyperparameter
C045.definition: Hyperparameter is a value, such as alpha, that determines the strength of momentum. This strength is set externally and influences how the optimization process behaves.

C046.name: Adam optimizer (Adam)
C046.definition: Adam optimizer (Adam) is a popular example of a type of momentum used within gradient descent. This optimizer is commonly used in deep learning applications.

C047.name: Differentiable
C047.definition: Differentiable describes a function that possesses a derivative at every point, which is a mathematical property required for calculating slopes and performing optimization.

C048.name: Exploding gradients
C048.definition: Exploding gradient occurs when the gradient increases toward infinity as the minimizer is approached. This results in highly unstable updates, making it difficult to actually hit the minimum.

C049.name: Vanishing gradient
C049.definition: Vanishing gradient is a condition where the gradient becomes extremely small as the minimum is approached, causing the training progress to be very slow. This slow progress can be dominated by noise in the training batches.

C050.name: Multiple local minima
C050.definition: Multiple local minima refers to a loss landscape that is not guaranteed to be convex, meaning it may contain several low-loss regions. When this occurs, the initial model parameters greatly influence which minimum the optimization process finds.

C051.name: Convexity
C051.definition: Convexity is a property of a function, such as a loss landscape, that allows for the assumption of a single minimum. When a function is convex, all gradients point toward that single minimum.

C052.name: Evolution strategy
C052.definition: Evolution strategy is a gradient-like method that finds locally loss-minimizing directions in parameter space. It achieves this by sampling small perturbations around existing parameter values and moving toward perturbations that achieve lower loss.

C053.name: Gradient clipping
C053.definition: Gradient clipping is a mechanism used to help manage peakiness or pointiness in a loss function. It works by scaling back the gradient if it exceeds a predefined large value, essentially placing a clipping filter on the gradient.

C054.name: Gaussian error linear unit
C054.definition: Gaussian error linear unit (GeLU) is a non-linearity that takes the parameters multiplied by the cumulative distribution function for the Gaussian distribution. This function is everywhere continuous, everywhere differentiable, and everywhere smooth.

C055.name: Loss function
C055.definition: Loss function is a function used in training that measures the difference between the predicted output and the actual target. Loss functions can sometimes be set up to have negative values.

C056.name: Computation graph
C056.definition: Computation graph is a graph of different functional transformations where each transformation is represented as a node. Stringing these nodes together allows for the performance of useful computation.

C057.name: Directed acyclic graph
C057.definition: Directed acyclic graph is a graph where information flows only in one direction along any given edge, and the graph contains no loops or cycles.

C058.name: Forward pass
C058.definition: Forward pass is the process of sending data forward through the network. This involves computing the outputs and calculating the overall loss.

C059.name: Cost
C059.definition: Cost is the overall calculation of the loss across all of the data. Cost is also a mechanism used to evaluate the optimality of the model.

C060.name: Jacobian formulation
C060.definition: The Jacobian formulation is a method used to calculate the partial derivative when the output is a vector and the input is a vector. This formulation results in a matrix whose size is determined by the size of the output by the size of the input.

C061.name: Partial derivative
C061.definition: A partial derivative is the rate of change of a function with respect to one specific variable while holding all other variables constant. When the input is a matrix and the output is a scalar, the resulting derivative is also a matrix.

C062.name: Transposed
C062.definition: Transposed refers to the operation of flipping the rows and columns of a matrix. This operation changes the dimensions of the matrix, which is noted when taking certain derivatives.

C063.name: Chain rule
C063.definition: The chain rule is a method used to find the derivative of a composite function, where one function is nested inside another. It involves multiplying the derivative of the outer function by the derivative of the inner function.

C064.name: Backwards pass
C064.definition: Backward pass is the iterative computation of loss derivatives, moving from the top layer down to the input. This process determines how much each parameter contributed to the overall loss.

C065.name: Layer output gradient (L)
C065.definition: Layer output gradient (L) is a matrix that tracks the gradient of the layer outputs with regard to the layer inputs. This matrix indicates which way the parameters need to change to move in the maximal direction of optimization.

C066.name: Cost gradient (g)
C066.definition: Cost gradient (g) is a row vector representing the gradient of the cost with respect to the activations. This vector essentially states the partial derivative of the cost with respect to the input of that layer.

C067.name: Merging
C067.definition: Merging is an operation that combines functional components to move forward through a directed-acyclic graph. When propagating a gradient back through a merge, one must track the gradient with respect to the correct input variables.

C068.name: Branching
C068.definition: Branching is the process of splitting up or duplicating information within a network. When propagating a gradient back through a branch, the gradients from both paths are summed and sent back through the input.

C069.name: Parameter sharing
C069.definition: Parameter sharing occurs when the parameters are reused across different components of a network, rather than having separate parameters for each component. This allows the network to reuse parameters, such as those pre-trained on ImageNet, in multiple parts of the network.

C070.name: Software 2.0
C070.definition: Software 2.0 is a concept where the software defines a space of possible systems, and the goal is to optimize within that space to build the specific system needed to solve a problem.

C071.name: Feature engineering
C071.definition: Feature engineering is a process where humans build explicit constraints into how the data might be processed before it is fed into a simple neural network.

C072.name: Optimizing inputs
C072.definition: Optimizing inputs involves considering how the cost changes by modifying the input data while keeping the network's parameters fixed. This approach allows for changes to the input, such as changing input pixels.

C073.name: Embedding
C073.definition: Embedding is a mapping that transforms a high-dimensional or complex input, such as an image, into a low-dimensional representation. Embedding is essentially the use of a pre-trained neural network to provide a low-rank representation of the input data.

C074.name: Attention block
C074.definition: Attention block is a component generally defined for a transformer that includes projections into a shared space. This block also includes a projection out into the space where the information is utilized.
